extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patentees, and third parties considering Post-Grant Review (PGR) before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on initiating and litigating a Post-Grant Review (PGR) at the USPTO Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), including filing timing, institution threshold, allowable grounds, procedural opportunities, and possible outcomes. Intended for parties (and their counsel) evaluating or defending against PGR petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation by petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR is initiated by the filing of a petition with the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proceeding begins when a third party files a petition with the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). This is analogous to an inter partes review (IPR) in procedure (filing a petition to initiate review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing deadline (time bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR must be filed within nine months of the patent’s issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike an IPR, which may be filed after the nine-month mark, a PGR is subject to a strict nine-month post-issuance filing window. Timely filing is therefore a jurisdictional/eligibility requirement for PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution threshold — reasonable likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must demonstrate there is a reasonable likelihood that at least one of the claims is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB will review the petition to determine whether the reasonable-likelihood standard is met as a predicate to instituting a PGR. This is analogous to institution standards used in other PTAB proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for PGR may challenge validity on additional grounds compared to an IPR, including anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, and indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR allows broader substantive challenges than IPR: in addition to the common prior-art grounds (anticipation and obviousness), petitioners may assert non-prior-art statutory grounds such as lack of written description, lack of enablement, and indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner response opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner in a PGR has an opportunity to respond to the petitioner’s arguments and present counterarguments and evidence to support the patent’s validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a petition is filed, the patent owner can submit a response to contest the petition’s merits and introduce evidence and arguments aimed at preserving claim validity during PTAB review.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB review and decision outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB will conduct a review of the patent and consider the petitioner’s arguments and any evidence presented, and will issue a decision on whether the challenged claims are patentable or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTAB finds claims unpatentable, they may be cancelled or amended. The PTAB’s decision resolves the instituted grounds as to the challenged claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel consequences for petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner in a PGR may be subject to estoppel, which may bar them from challenging the patent in subsequent proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PGR can adjudicate validity issues, a petitioner who participates and receives adverse findings may be estopped from raising the same grounds or arguments in later proceedings; parties should weigh this risk when deciding to file.
